result.summary: Persephone is snatched by Aidoneus (Hades) while picking flowers, with Zeus's consent, and only Hecate and Helios hear her cry. Demeter searches for nine days, learns the truth from Helios, and in anger leaves Olympus to wander disguised until she reaches Eleusis, where Celeus's daughters find her at a well.

scenes.title: The Narcissus Snare
scenes.summary: The hymn opens by naming Demeter and her daughter. Persephone picks flowers with the Oceanids and reaches for the narcissus, and the earth opens.
scenes.stakes: Persephone is about to be seized and lose her freedom and her mother.

scenes.title: The Abduction
scenes.summary: Aidoneus carries Persephone off in his chariot as she cries to her father. Only Hecate and Helios hear her, while Zeus sits apart, accepting offerings.
scenes.stakes: Persephone is carried off unwilling and cannot be rescued.

scenes.title: Demeter Searches for Her Daughter
scenes.summary: Demeter hears her daughter's cry, tears her veil and searches nine days with torches. On the tenth dawn Hecate tells her she heard but did not see the abductor.
scenes.stakes: Demeter risks losing her daughter forever and wears herself out with grief.

scenes.title: Helios Tells the Truth
scenes.summary: Demeter asks Helios, who sees all. He names Zeus as the giver and Hades as the taker, and urges her to accept the match.
scenes.stakes: Demeter needs the truth to find her daughter; Helios risks nothing but her anger.

scenes.title: Disguised at Eleusis
scenes.summary: Demeter, angry with Zeus, leaves Olympus and wanders disguised as an old woman. She sits by the Maiden Well at Eleusis, where Celeus's four daughters see her.
scenes.stakes: Demeter is estranged from the gods and hides her identity among mortals.

alias_notes.explanation: Aidoneus is a variant of Hades, lord of the dead; the text also calls him Host of Many and Ruler of Many.
Deo is another name for Demeter.
Sentences 5 and 7 use this title for Zeus; sentences 3 and 8 use it for Hades.

notable_quotes.reason: The narcissus is a radiant lure, and all creation laughs for joy before the abduction.
States that gods are not easily recognized by mortals.

analysis.text: The abduction of Persephone brings out loss, a mother's grief and the power of Zeus's will, and it sets up the origin of the seasons and the Eleusinian rites.
The hymn is the main literary source for the Eleusinian Mysteries, the secret cult at Eleusis near Athens.

legacy.text: The myth of Demeter and Persephone became the standard ancient explanation for the seasons and inspired many later poems and paintings, such as Ovid's retelling and Rossetti's Proserpine.

fun_facts.text: The hymn survives in a single medieval manuscript found in Moscow in 1777, and it has gaps (lacunae) such as the one marked after line 36.

language_notes.text: Aidoneus is a name for Hades, lord of the dead. 'Rapt' means seized and carried off by force.
'Host of Many' is an epithet of Hades, the one who receives all the dead as guests. 'Bloom-like' means flower-fresh.
'Car' means chariot. 'Nysa' is a legendary plain whose location the hymn does not fix.
'Son of Cronos' here refers to Hades, who was a brother of Zeus; Zeus is also called Son of Cronos later. The '2505' is a stray footnote marker.
'Bright-coiffed' means with shining headdress or hair. 'Coiffed' refers to hairstyle.
'Lacuna' marks a gap in the surviving manuscript, where lines are missing.
Deo is another name for Demeter. Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods.
"Do you at least regard me" means "show me some regard or respect"; Demeter appeals to past favours to Helios.
"Scion" means offspring or descendant; here it is Persephone, called the sweet offspring of Demeter's body.
"Son of Hyperion" is Helios, the Sun. Hyperion was a Titan, and the title serves as a patronymic.
"Buxom" here is old usage meaning obliging or yielding, not the modern sense; she is to be his wife.
"That third share" refers to the division of the cosmos among the three sons of Cronos: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld.
"Aidoneus" is a name for Hades; "Ruler of Many" is an epithet for him as lord of the dead.
"Chiding" means a sharp command or rebuke, here Helios urging on his horses.
"Maiden Well" was a well at Eleusis, traditionally linked to this myth, where women drew water.
"Winged words" is a Homeric formula for speech that flies from speaker to listener.

context_notes.text: The Oceanids are daughters of the Titan Oceanus, the river encircling the world. They are Persephone's playmates.
Hecate is a goddess associated with night, magic and crossroads. Helios is the sun god, who sees everything as he crosses the sky.
Tearing the veil and discarding the cloak are signs of mourning in ancient Greek custom.
Torches suggest night searching and also recall torchlit rites later connected with Demeter's mysteries.
Helios, the Sun god, travels across the sky each day and so sees everything on earth, making him the natural witness.
Hades is brother of Zeus and Demeter, so Zeus gave his niece Persephone to her uncle in marriage.
Eleusis was a town near Athens, later famed for the Eleusinian Mysteries, rites honouring Demeter and Persephone.
Demeter disguises herself as an old woman past childbearing, a figure who might plausibly be hired as a nurse or housekeeper.

literary_notes.text: Stock descriptions such as 'deep-bosomed' and 'lady of the golden sword' fit the oral epic style and identify each figure.
Heaven, earth and sea 'laughed for joy' at the flower, giving nature human emotion and stressing its dangerous beauty.
Persephone calls the flower a 'lovely toy', but it is a trap, so her delight leads straight to her seizure.
Zeus sits calmly receiving offerings while his daughter screams, showing his complicity and distance from her suffering.
Demeter rushing 'like a wild-bird' over land and sea conveys frantic, helpless speed in her grief.
Demeter directly addresses the all-seeing sun, framing her plea as an appeal to a witness who cannot be deceived.
The swift chariot is compared to long-winged birds, conveying how quickly Helios departs after delivering his news.
Demeter's withdrawal from Olympus shows her anger and her willingness to defy Zeus, unlike Helios, who urges acceptance.
The remark that gods are hard for mortals to recognise hints at the later revelation of Demeter's divine identity.
